extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers learning how to approach literature; educators, editors, and printers interested in orthography and proofreading
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for (1) how students and readers should select and read works of literature (methods, use of guides, following intertextual leads, translation awareness) and (2) norms and practical criteria for spelling reform, printing accuracy, proofreading, errata handling, and improving personal efficiency by forethought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a reading method suited to prior knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Three methods of beginning literary study are described: (1) map literature from one's previous reading to find inner boundaries and points of departure; (2) take the first attractive unread book at hand and let it lead to others; (3) for readers with scant previous reading, be furnished with a guide who will set feet in right paths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the method that fits your background: use prior reading to identify directions of study; follow attractive unread books when you already have general knowledge; seek a guide/companion if your reading has been perfunctory. Each method will suggest many further points of departure rather than a single path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a guide/companion to set literary bearings
rubrics_metrics.description: A student whose previous reading is scanty must be furnished with a guide who shall set his feet in the right paths, give him his bearings in literature, and inspire him with a love for the beauty and grandeur of the scenery disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer guides that offer delightful companionship and invite the reader to share favorite walks in 'Bookland' (example: Hazlitt's "Lectures on the English Poets"). A good guide should introduce the field, give outlook, and train the reader toward independent exploration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guides should present authors with illustrative specimens and comparative groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable literary guide does not content itself with mere estimates and characterizations but furnishes illustrative specimens of the poems discussed and often presents authors in pairs or groups to show contrasted merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective criticism introduces form and difference (what poetry is, how forms move us, how they differ from eloquence/romance), uses paired comparisons (e.g., Chaucer and Spenser; Shakespeare and Milton), and supplies passages so readers can judge for themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow intertextual leads to primary works and related literatures
rubrics_metrics.description: When a guide draws attention to an author or poem, the student should lay it aside and make excursions into the primary works and related literatures that the guide points to (e.g., reading Cervantes leads to romances of chivalry, then to Fielding, Thackeray, Dickens, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a guide to launch autonomous reading: take up the works mentioned, pursue historical/cultural subjects raised by a text (e.g., Charlemagne, Moors), and explore cognate languages and literatures if necessary. The guide's highest mission is to inspire independent reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read works in their relations and contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not read a book as an isolated fragment; read it 'in its relations'—historical, literary, linguistic, and cultural connections enrich understanding (illustrated by the example of reading Don Quixote leading to many related inquiries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On encountering references in a work, read the referenced materials (romances, historical background) and compare later/earlier influences; examine translations and their differences to understand changes in language, style, and ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of and compare translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations differ enormously in language, literary style, and ideals of rendering (example: Shelton, Motteux, and Ormsby translations of Cervantes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading translated works, compare versions to note linguistic and stylistic differences; if deeply interested, consider learning the original language to access authorial voice directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: A guide should train the reader toward independent exploration
rubrics_metrics.description: The highest mission of a guide is to inspire and train its reader to do without it—so that the student will become eager and able to pursue literature alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guides as temporary scaffolding: follow their leads into the library and let personal curiosity and handling of books determine further reading until the problem becomes not what to read but what to resist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling/orthography should be phonetic where practical
rubrics_metrics.description: To the philologist, spelling is the application of an alphabet to the words of a language; given a scientific alphabet, spelling as a problem vanishes because there is only one possible spelling for any spoken word and one possible pronunciation for any written word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a spelling system in which letters reliably represent sounds (phonetic/phonemic orthography). Examples cited: modern Swedish and German reforms that made spelling closely reflect pronunciation (Swedish 'dem' vs older 'them'; German 'Brot' vs 'Brod'/'Brodt').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize representational practicality over visible etymology when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: If a spelling system cannot both indicate pronunciation and etymology, it is more practical to indicate pronunciation and relegate etymology to the dictionary; Europeans often accept loss of visible etymology for greater phonetic accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept occasional loss of apparent etymological links in spelling (e.g., Swedish 'byrå' vs French 'bureau') if doing so simplifies and regularizes spelling for users and learners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement orthographic reform gradually and preserve classic editions
rubrics_metrics.description: English is certain to have eventually a more scientific spelling, but the change should be spread over decades and will be too gradual to affect business appreciably; standard old editions will continue to be prized while popular editions will use contemporary spelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan reforms with historical editions preserved for interest; issue contemporary-spelling editions for general use when metre and rhyme permit; expect slow transition and avoid sudden, wholesale replacement of existing printed works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthographic reform aims to reduce educational waste and economic cost
rubrics_metrics.description: Current irregularities in English spelling cost the English-speaking world enormously in wasted instructional time and commercial inefficiency (an estimated 'hundred million dollars a year' lost to silent letters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the economic and educational benefits of simplified/phonetic spelling as part of the argument for change: shorter schooling for children learning to read/spell and reduced errors in commerce and official usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing should aim at near-perfection; misprints are serious
rubrics_metrics.description: In the printing office the standard is nothing less than perfection; misprints (printer's errors, errors of the press) are conspicuous and range from trivial to meaning-reversing mistakes with legal or financial consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat all typographical deviations as potentially important. Recognize that responsibility for errors is shared between author and printer, but submission of proof fixes final responsibility on the author—therefore both parties must be diligent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading must check for subtle but consequential typographic errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors such as a turned letter, omitted punctuation, separation of a word into two, mixed paragraphs, or wrong lineation in poetry can reverse meaning or spoil metre and emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofreaders must check every element: individual letters, punctuation, word divisions, paragraph order, and the correct assignment of lines and speakers in poetry. Even apparently small changes (omission of 'not' in a commandment) can have grave effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform proof correction after locking forms and before final printing
rubrics_metrics.description: Some blunders occur when forms are locked or when sheets are mixed; proofs should be read after these stages so errors in typesetting or composition can be caught before mass printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt production-stage checks: read proofs after composition and after any corrections; where errors are found in press, supply errata slips or reprint corrected sheets; offer a list of errata if full correction is not possible immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle errata transparently and provide corrected material to purchasers
rubrics_metrics.description: When errors are discovered, the list of errata may be printed as an extension of the text or supplied on a separate slip or sheet and inserted in the book or supplied to purchasers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide purchasers with errata sheets or corrected reprints; in some historical cases errata sheets have become part of collector value, but the practical aim is prompt and clear correction for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution when correcting errors to avoid introducing new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The most baffling device is to cause a new error in the process of correcting an old one; residuary misprints are a persistent risk and can compound problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections should be checked carefully against original manuscripts and context. Example: an intended reading 'tilt' was changed to 'lilt' and then back again—editing decisions must verify authorial intent and manuscript evidence before altering printed text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printing of poetry requires special typographical care
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is liable to unique printing errors (dropped words, lines assigned to wrong speakers, stanza breaks lost) that can damage metre, emphasis, and sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting and proofreading poetry, verify lineation, stanza divisions, speaker attributions in dialogue poems, and exact replication of metre-sensitive punctuation; ensure reproductions do not disrupt rhythm or meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on mechanical typesetting; human oversight remains necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Typesetting machines (linotype, etc.) are not protection against the Imp of the Perverse; mechanical processes can introduce or fail to catch errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain human proofreaders and final checks even with mechanized composition; recognize that some errors (mixed paragraphs, upside-down lines) arise from processes machines alone do not prevent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply forethought to increase personal efficiency and reveal latent powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Forethought is a controlling principle wider than mere thought; it can evoke latent and unexpected powers, extend to all functions of the soul, and even affect bodily energy and health. Responsibility is a stimulus that can bring out unrecognized ability (examples: Grant and Lincoln).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate forethought in personal management and assign responsibility as a method to test and develop abilities. Be realistic: foresight cannot create ability where none exists, and individuals have unequal endowments; the aim is to discover and mobilize existing reserves rather than invent new capacity.
